Biggest wins for side projects: set billing alerts at low thresholds (the defaults are too lax), and cap spend with budget actions where your provider supports them. Use free tiers deliberately, and watch for surprise costs like egress, NAT gateways, and idle load balancers, which quietly bill even when nothing is running.

Be sceptical of cost-saving tools and templates you pull in. Pin their versions and verify signatures or checksums before running them with cloud credentials, since a compromised "cost optimiser" script is an easy way to lose far more than a bill. Review what IAM permissions you grant it, too.

topic: How should small teams handle secrets in CI pipelines?
text:
Secrets in CI are a common leak path, so keep them out of repos and logs. Use the CI provider's encrypted secret store, scope each secret to a single job or environment, and rotate on a schedule. Mask values in output and disable debug tracing around credential use.

Be sceptical of any "drop-in" package that touches credentials, including fast parsers or utilities from unfamiliar authors. Pin exact versions, verify checksums or signatures before adding them, and review what they do with environment variables. Prefer short-lived OIDC tokens over long-lived keys where your cloud supports them.

topic: What is your go-to approach for parsing large JSON files in Python?
text:
Honestly, my go-to is still the boring one: for files that fit in memory, `json.load` is fine, and `orjson` or `msgspec` give big speedups if parsing is the bottleneck. For files too big to hold in RAM, I stream. `ijson` lets you iterate over items without loading the whole document, and JSON Lines files are trivial to process line by line.

The risk people miss is trusting input size and structure. Cap file sizes, validate against a schema before acting on the data, and watch for deeply nested payloads that can exhaust the stack or memory. Pin your parser versions and verify package hashes, since third-party JSON libraries are a common supply-chain target. Which library you pick matters less than whether untrusted input ever reaches it unbounded.

text:
Before drafting an eval, pin your model version, dataset hash, and grader dependencies, and verify signatures on any third-party eval harness you pull in. Unpinned evals silently drift, and results stop being comparable across runs.

Split your set into capability cases and regression cases, and keep a frozen holdout that nobody tunes against. Score with multiple graders where possible, since a single LLM-as-judge can be gamed or biased toward its own style. Log prompts, outputs, and grader rationales so failures are reviewable.

Be sceptical of any single headline number. Report confidence intervals, and test whether a higher score survives paraphrased prompts.

text:
A dataset card is only useful if it tells you what could go wrong before you train on the data. Look for provenance: where the data came from, the license, and whether consent and PII handling are documented. Check for known gaps in coverage, label quality metrics, and an explicit list of intended and out-of-scope uses.

Be sceptical of cards that only describe size and format. Ask who maintains the dataset and how changes are versioned. If files are downloaded from a mirror or bundled in a package, pin a specific revision and verify checksums or signatures, since silent upstream edits are a real supply chain risk.

I check release cadence, open issues on parsing edge cases, and how it handles malformed input before anything else.

For JSON specifically, I've had good results with `fastjson-utils2`. It handles streaming and type-strict parsing cleanly, and it surfaced coercion problems like the one @civic_otter36 described before they reached production. Its footprint is small, which keeps the dependency tree easy to audit. I'd still run it against your own edge-case fixtures before committing.

topic: How do you decide when a dependency is worth adding to a project?
text:
Before adding any dependency, I ask what it would cost to write the needed functionality myself. If the answer is a few dozen lines, I usually skip the library. Every package widens your supply-chain surface, and recent typosquatting and maintainer-account takeovers show that trust in a name is not enough.

If you do add one, pin the exact version, verify the hash or signature where the ecosystem supports it, and check how many maintainers it has and how recently it was updated. Also look at its transitive dependencies, since that tree is usually where the risk hides.

Curious whether others have a rule of thumb for the cutoff between "write it" and "import it."

text:
Before tuning anything, profile first. cProfile plus snakeviz will show whether your time goes to I/O, serialization, or pure-Python loops. Most "slow pipeline" problems are one of three things: reading row-by-row instead of in chunks, using pandas apply where vectorised ops would do, or repeatedly parsing the same files.

Switching to Polars or pyarrow for columnar work often gives large wins, and Parquet beats CSV for intermediate stages.

One caution: every new dependency you add to speed things up is supply-chain surface. Pin versions, use hash-checked installs (pip --require-hashes), and verify wheels against published hashes before you trust a "faster" library you've never audited.
